Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings: Acute onset watery, non-bloody diarrhea with intermittent LLQ crampy pain following restaurant meal; initial vomiting and subjective fever; tolerating fluids; no hematochezia; one household contact with vomiting only. Past history significant for well-controlled asthma on inhaler.
- Impression: Acute gastroenteritis. DDx supports a likely viral etiology; a bacterial foodborne cause remains possible given timing after takeaway. No red flags (no blood, able to hydrate).
- Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis, likely viral; bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis possible.
- Management priorities: Maintain hydration; symptom control; temporary work cessation to rest and reduce transmission; reassess if not improving in 3–4 days; consider stool studies if persistent/worsening.

Management Plan

- Oral rehydration: Encourage fluids; pharmacist ORS (e.g., Dioralyte) recommended to replace electrolytes.
- Symptom relief: Paracetamol/acetaminophen for fever/aches (advised “two tablets up to four times daily”; strength not documented).
- Activity/work: Advise rest and time off work for 2–3 days.
- Monitoring and follow-up: If symptoms not improving within 3–4 days or if worsening (e.g., inability to keep fluids down, blood in stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain), return for reassessment. If ongoing, consider stool sample testing. No antibiotics indicated at this stage.
- Patient education: Clear plan discussed; patient agreed and had no further questions.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded.
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) – Likelihood: High. Justification: Short-duration watery diarrhea, initial vomiting, subjective fever, household contact with vomiting; typically self-limited.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis/foodborne infection (e.g., Salmonella, ETEC, Campylobacter) – Likelihood: Moderate. Justification: Onset ~1 day after restaurant meal; watery diarrhea with crampy pain and early fever; absence of blood does not exclude.
- Toxin-mediated food poisoning (Staph aureus/Bacillus cereus) – Likelihood: Low. Justification: Restaurant exposure and early vomiting compatible, but typical incubation is hours and course is shorter than observed.

- Internal contradictions between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear but some responses were brief; no examination findings or vitals documented.
